maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY STATEMENT OP ACTING SECRETARY OP STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

speechtext:
On the order for motions:
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs): I should like at this time to make a brief statement which was asked for by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) on October 4. as reported at page 756 of Hansard. The hon. member asked:
Will the acting leader of the house be in a position to make a statement within a few days regarding the St. Lawrence waterway, in view of the message of President Truman to Congress yesterday recommending an early start?
In reply the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) stated that the question would be referred to the Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs. I have had the statement prepared and I think it should be communicated to the house.
The Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Basin agreement was signed at Ottawa, March 19, 1941. It makes provision for the development of navigation and power resources within the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence basin for the joint account of the peoples of Canada and the United States. Generally, it covers the same fields as the Niagara convention of 1929 and the St. Lawrence waterway treaty of 1932.
2.	Immediately after the signing of the agreement, a white paper, including correspondence and documents relating to the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence basin development, was tabled in the House of Commons on March 21, 1941.
For the convenience of the members of the house I am tabling additional copies, both in English and in French, of the white paper: Correspondence and documents relating to The Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Basin development, 1938-1941.
I am also tabling copies, both in English and in French, of an additional white paper: Correspondence and documents relating to The Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Basin development, supplement No. 1; (i) legal opinions; (ii) summary of outstanding features.
3.	The agreement provided for ratification and it was made subject to approval by the parliament of Canada and the congress of the United States of America. In this respect, it differed from the 1932 treaty which required the observance of "constitutional methods"

St. Lawrence Waterway
before ratification. The 1932 treaty could only be ratified by the President of the United States if approved by a two-thirds majority of the senate. The present agreement could only be ratified by him if it were approved by joint resolution of both the senate and the house of representatives.
4.	Accordingly, the agreement was submitted to the house of representatives in 1941 and referred to the committee on rivers and harbours. It failed, however, to obtain the necessary congressional approval and no action was taken by way of ratification either in 1941 or in succeeding years.
5.	An attempt was made in the senate of the United States in 1944 to obtain the necessary approval by the adoption of what would have been a joint resolution, but it was unsuccessful.
6.	Upon the initiative of the President of the United States of America, a joint resolution was introduced in the senate and in the house of representatives on October 2 of this year. The procedure followed is somewhat different from that which was adopted in earlier years and the joint resolution is fundamentally different. The earlier resolutions had been designed to provide for approval of the entire agreement with a view to ratification of the agreement and proceeding with the project. The joint resolution as presented both in the senate and in the house of representatives is different from the earlier resolutions in the following respects:
(a)	The resolution approves the agreement with the exception of articles VII and IX and authorizes the President to fulfil the undertakings, other than those which are contained in these articles, upon approval of the agreement, with the exeception of the articles in question, by reciprocal or concurrent legislation in Canada.
(b)	The resolution indicates that it is the view of congress that the President should negotiate with Canada a treaty or treaties covering the subject matter of articles VII and IX, including the provision with respect to perpetual navigation rights on the great lakes, on the connecting channels and canals, and in the wholly Canadian sections of the St. Lawrence river, and provisions for the amendment of the Boundary Waters Treaty of 1909 with respect to the diversion of waters at the Niagara river, and should submit the treaty for the advice and consent of the senate.
(c)	The president is directed to provide for the investigation of the feasibility of making the project self-liquidating by the imposition
47696-68J
of reasonable charges or tolls on the foreign commerce of the two countries utilizing the facilities.
(d)	Provision is made with respect to the appropriation of funds and there is a declaration to the effect that no exchange of notes under article I, section 4 of the agreement is to impose additional financial or other obligations on the United States. (This refers to a power enabling the governments, by exchange of notes, to prescribe rules and regulations for the conduct of the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Basin commission, to expand or abridge its powers and duties, to reduce, or after reduction, to increase the number of members, and to wind up the commission. The declaration does not, however, change the obligations of the governments in any respect, as the limitations would be implied in the absence of an express provision of this sort.)
(e)	The President is authorized, by arrangement with the government of the state of New York, to transfer the power facilities to the appropriate agency of the state in accordance with certain principles and there is a proviso that the arrangement must be consistent with the laws of the United States and protect the interests of the United States and of other states and also that the arrangement is to be subject to approval by congress and the legislature of the state of New York.
7.	For the information of the members of the house, I am tabling three copies, in English, of the joint resolution which has been introduced both in the senate and in the house of representatives of the United States of America and, if this course meets with the approval of the members of. the house, the text of this joint resolution could be printed in Votes and Proceedings. May I take it that I have the unanimous consent of the house?
Some bon. MEMBERS:	Consent.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: To continue:
8.	If the joint resolution is approved by congress, it may be necessary for the dominion government to confer with the governments of the province of Ontario and Quebec. The existing arrangements, so far as Ontario is concerned, are embodied in the agreement at page 11 of the first white paper and in the correspondence at pages 43-45. The arrangements with the province of Quebec are embodied in the correspondence at pages 66-72. Consideration of the question as to whether the modifications involved in the procedure now before the congress of the United States of America present any difficulty from the Canadian point of view must, necessarily, be deferred until a later stage.
St. Lawrence Waterway

9.	It is difficult, if not impossible, to forecast the time which will be taken (a) in dealing with the matter by the congress of the United States of America; (b) in negotiating the additional treaty, and (c) in consultations with the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, but there would seem to be a good deal of doubt as to whether the matter is likely to reach a stage at which it can be presented to parliament during the present session. In the meantime, the proceedings in congress do not in any way of course commit the parliament or government of Canada in any respect.

speechtext:
As I followed the minister's statement, he indicated that the agreements which had been before the two countries, with the exception of articles YII and IX, were now being submitted to congress, through presidential action. The minister, however, did not make one point clear. Did the President of the United States or anyone acting on behalf of the government of that country submit the agreement, with the exception of articles VII and IX, to the Canadian government or any of its members, before it was presented to congress in the changed form in which it appears to have come before that body? In other words, it seems to me the President of the United States is now submitting to the congress something different from that which had originally been agreed upon between the two nations. I am wondering whether he, or someone representing the United States, had consulted with the Canadian government in respect of those changes, before the submission was made to congress.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I would not be in a position to give a positive answer to my hon.. friend at the moment. My understanding, however, is that there is no intention of modifying the substance of the agreement, but rather that this proceeding has been adopted because it was felt there that with respect to all the subject matter of the agreement, not including articles VII and IX, it could be dealt with by joint resolution of the two houses of congress. It was felt, however, that with respect to articles VII and IX there should be a formal treaty. This of course would require for purposes of ratification a two-thirds vote of the senate of the United States. There were conversations, or exchanges of views, with respect to the procedure to be adopted, and Canada voiced no objection to the attempt being made to have the matter submitted in the form that is now contemplated in the United States. We. of course, will await further developments there before

determining what the subject matter of our further negotiations with Ontario and Quebec should be.

subtopic: ARRANGEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES

speechtext:
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs):	Mr. Speaker, there is another matter with respect to which considerable public interest has been manifested and which I think should be made

Questions
public just as early as can be. It has to do with the extradition arrangements between Canada and the United States.
Extradition arrangements between Canada and the United States have in the past been based upon treaties between the latter and the United Kingdom government and extending over a long period of years. A new extradition treaty was negotiated between the United States and the United Kingdom some years ago. It did not extend to Canada, and provision was made to preserve extradition arrangements under the old treaties in so far as Canada was concerned.
A new treaty with Canada was signed on April 29, 1942 and was approved by the United States senate in May of that year. On June 6, the president of the United States provided for ratification. The matter was about to be brought to the attention of. parliament for approval when protests were made from financial organizations from coast to coast in respect of possible offences relating to dealings in securities, and further action was deferred.
An endeavour has since been made to formulate a protocol to overcome the substantial objections which were raised. It was recognized that it would be impossible to induce the United States to change their security laws so as to permit free marketing of securities within the United States without compliance with laws made for the protection of United States investors. On the other hand, it was recognized that protection must be given to Canadian business men engaged in legitimate business within this country and to Canadian publishers of advertising or other matter. Negotiations have been carried on with the United States representatives, and a protocol has been signed designed to carry out these objectives.
For the information of the members of the house I am tabling copies in English and in French of treaty series 1942 No. 10, treaty for the extradition of criminals concluded between Canada and the United States of America, Washington, April 29, 1942, and copies in English and in French of protocol annexed to the treaty for the extradition of criminals between the United States of America and Canada which was signed at Ottawa, October 3, 1945.
A resolution will be introduced in due course in both houses of parliament which will provide an opportunity for full discussion of this matter.

1.	What clauses of the prison reform commission report have been adopted by the government since the report was tabled?
2.	Who is in charge of federal prisons, is it the Minister of Justice or the Solicitor General, and what is the division of authority between them, if any, herein?
3.	Who appoints those in charge of these institutions and the staff, and what qualifications have they in this work before appointment?
4.	What inspection is there of these institutions, and how many visits have been made by the minister in charge?
5.	What practical experience have the chief officers of the department in this work before appointment?
6.	Do grand juries visit these institutions and make a report? If so, to whom?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I should like to deal with this question orally. I have no doubt that the first question refers to the report of the royal commission on penitentiaries. No clauses of that report have been adopted. Full detailed particulars of the recommendations of the royal commission which have been acted upon by the department were furnished in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Broadview on April 4, 1945. There have been few, if any, additional recommendations acted upon since that time.
In reply to part 2 of the question, I would say that the Minister of Justice is in charge of federal prisons; he is the minister responsible for the administration of the penitentiaries, under section three of the Penitentiary Act.
In reply to part 3, first I would say that the minister is appointed by the governor in council. The appointment of officers is made pursuant to sections 20 and 20A of the Penitentiary Act, as amended by chapter 27 of the statutes of Canada, 1933. Wardens usually have years of experience in penitentiary administration before appointment, and the staff do not necessarily have previous experience in penitentiary work before appointment.
As to qualifications, wardens are usually promoted to that position, but occasionally one is appointed without previous experience. subtopic: ENCOURAGEMENT OF USE OF HARBOUR AND PORT FACILITIES
ENCOURAGEMENT OF USE OF HARBOUR AND PORT FACILITIES
speechtext:
That in the opinion of this house the government should take into immediate consideration the advisability of encouraging the fullest possible use of the harbour and port facilities at Churchill, Manitoba, or the transferring of the management and control of the said port to a joint board appointed by the governments cf Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta.
Port of Churchill

He said: Mr. Speaker, this resolution was placed on the order paper because it is of growing importance to northern Canada and to the future economy of our country. I do not know how much latitude we are permitted in dealing with resolutions of this kind, but it is important for us to realize that our economy is gradually spreading to the northern sections of this country.
It is a significant fact that in 1812 the first settlers in western Canada came by way of Hudson bay to the spot where Winnipeg now stands. Those original settlers did not forget the route by which they landed at the gateway to the west, and for many years after the colony became firmly established there was a growing demand that they be given an outlet to Hudson bay and a connection with their mother country.
Prior to this first settlement the inland sea known as Hudson bay had its waters furrowed by the keels of many ships belonging to the Hudson's Bay company. That the route was a safe one may be judged from the fact that the Hudson's Bay company took back to England a fabulous amount of wealth.
I think it is important that we should review briefly the history of Canada at this period. In those early days, after the fall of France in Canada, the history of this country was the history of the fur trade and the history of the fur trade was the history of two great companies, one English, the other Canadian. The Hudson's Bay company, with headquarters in London, England, sent its ships out from Europe to Hudson bay to carry with them the wares they brought from England in exchange for the furs they received from the natives along the shores and in the southern part of the northern territories. The Northwest company had their headquarters in Montreal. They, too, carried on a thriving trade with the natives in this country. However, it was found that the long route from Montreal to the head of the lakes had to be made by canoe over treacherous waterways and it was difficult terrain to traverse; it was very expensive.
History records the fact that is cost the Northwest company four times as much to *place their wares in England as it cost the Hudson's Bay company. Difficulties between the two companies became rife; competition was keen. In fact toward the end open conflit resulted. But the Hudson's Bay company bided its time. It was the sheer practicability of the Hudson bay route into the heart of America, that made competition

impracticable if not well-nigh impossible. The two companies finally composed their differences, with the result that the flag of the Hudson's Bay company was left on every trading post throughout the northwest.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that as time went on our governments of the past repeated in railway construction the same mistakes that led to the defeat of the Northwest company in the early fur trade in Canadian history. I wish to make it plain at this time, that we are not blaming anybody for these mistakes. It was only natural that they should occur, because our development first began from the shores of the St. Lawrence river. Canadian settlement first began at these points. Montreal and Toronto were thriving cities before the west was ever heard of; therefore it was only natural that the big interests in those places should want the trade from the northwest to flow to the financial coffers of Montreal and Toronto. We are not objecting. That was the attitude they took. But we want to point out that in accepting the building in Canada of a national transcontinental railway system to carry our goods east and west we completely ignored the most feasible and the most logical route, that to the northern sea.
We feel strongly that some time in the near future Hudson bay is going to be the principal sea lane between the old world and the new. I know there are many people who say that you cannot navigate Hudson bay and Hudson strait for more than three months of the year. I am going to allow that statement to pass for the time being, but I doubt it very much. I doubt it for this reason. It will be remembered that from 1914 to 1918, when there was great danger of German U-boats shutting off the north Atlantic, plans were ready to make full use of Hudson bay; and in the war just finished, when there was danger of long-range German U-boats cutting off the North Atlantic, it was also possible that we could have used Hudson bay.
In order to demonstrate the possibilities of this route, since the railroad is now completed to Churchill, I want to quote from some of the shipping authorities who have had boats going to the seaport of Port Churchill. I want to quote from the imperial committee on shipping. This is what they say:
As far as physical risks are concerned we are convinced that the Hudson bay route is not more dangerous, and in some respects less dangerous, than the St. Lawrence route.

Port oj Churchill
In making that statement I presume that the imperial committee is referring to the season in which shipping is carried on in Hudson bay.
May I now refer to the Dalgleish report on Hudson bay shipping. R. L. Dalgleish is the president of the Dalgleish Shipping Company of England. His boats were the first to sail into the Hudson bay to take wheat from that port after the railroad was completed in 1931. Here is what he has to say concerning the possibility of the Hudson bay route:
I loaded the first ship at Churchill eight years ago with wheat, and anyone who says that Port Churchill will not in course of time become one of the world's great ports does not know w'hat he is talking about.
That was in 1931, and again I presume that Mr. Dalgleish is referring to the navigational season in Hudson bay, which is from approximately the middle of June until the first week in October. But I wish to indicate to the administration the possibilities of extending that season to five or six months and perhaps at some time in the future to a year-round port. As proof of that, I wish to quote from an eminent Canadian geologist and explorer, Doctor Robert Bell, Fellow of the Royal Society, explorer of the northwest and a very high authority on northern navigation. He was sent to Hudson bay and Hudson strait by the federal government in, I believe, 1881, to investigate the possibilities of navigating Hudson bay and strait, and this is the report which he gave on returning from that area in 1881:
It is impossible that there should be at any time in the twelve months difficulty in navigating Hudson straits for they are upon tide water. In regard to the bay itself, there is no date for the opening or closing of navigation because the bay is open all the year round, like the ocean in corresponding latitudes. It is strictly correct to say that the bay is open during the winter. There is a margin of ice along the shallow- water, but it never extends so far but a man on the beach can see the open water on a clear morning. Bay ice. being light and rotten after it breaks away from the shore, offers little obstruction to the steamship.
That is the opinion of Doctor Bell in connection with the possibilities of making Hudson bay- a year-round port. I am not going to ask that the present administration do that immediately; I fully realize that it will take time to bring that about; but I want to point out that there are eminent explorers who believe Hudson bay can be made a year-round port, and I venture to say that we shouid approach the matter from that angle.
From 1880 until 1914 Canada expanded in a westward direction with the settlement of the plains in the western part of the country. From now on, I think we are going to expand more. We are going to see greater development in northern Canada than we have ever seen before. At the present moment the Hudson Bay railway runs 510 miles from the Pas. Manitoba, to Churchill, and over that 510 miles of steel, it is correct to say, there is not much traffic. But that railway runs through one of the richest mineral areas to be found anywhere on this continent. At places it does not pass directly through the area but it passes close by mineral fields which could be connected up by short lines of railway, and I have no doubt that within the next few years we shall see these developments take place.
Already at a place close to the Hudson Bayrailway, at Wekusko in northern Manitoba, development is being made in gold mining. I understand that a site for the town has already been laid out and some time in the future it will furnish homes for eight thousand people; and there is sufficient ore to last some fifty y-ears.
Some hon. members may ask, what is the use of our using this route when we have already three transcontinental railways in Canada capable of shipping all Canadian grain to the eastern seaboard? The answer is this. It is much cheaper to ship by sea than by rail. The sea route from Churchill, Manitoba, to European ports is approximately 100 sea miles farther than from the eastern seaboard, but the rail haul is much less, and it is the rail haul that is really expensive. From Saskatoon to Churchill is approximately 800 miles, and from Saskatoon to the head of the lakes is only slightly- greater; but it is another 1,200 miles to salt water, and that extra 1,200 miles must be made either by rail or by cargo boats across the great lakes. If you make it by cargo boat you have to shift your cargo several times before you finally get it on the ocean freighter at Montreal, and that costs money.
According to the grain commissioners, the use of this northern route will mean a saving to western Canada of seven cents a bushel, basis Port Churchill. Now seven cents a bushel is a very large saving on the grain of the western farmer. I want to suggest something that the government could do in order to increase that saving, should they find it convenient to make further use of the
Port of Churchill

Churchill route. At the present time the chief hold-up in connection with the use of the Hudson bay route is the excessively high insurance premiums charged on ships going into Hudson bay, and I should like to deal with the unfair insurance charges in connection with the bay route.
It is most important that something be done to bring to a reasonable figure the insurance rates on ships plying Hudson bay. At the moment the marine insurance rates are based on "whole-world" basis renewable yearly. These policies are subject to "institute warranties" which in actuality are agreements that the ships will not be taken into certain trade routes or into certain ports considered to involve extra risk. The British North American "warranty clause" provides that no ship may enter British North American ports, that is Canadian ports, with the exception of Vancouver, Prince Rupert, Halifax and Saint John, New Brunswick. Should a ship be routed to prohibited waters an additional fee must be paid, as laid down by the joint Hull committee. Then for vessels which wish to use the Hudson bay route a further and exorbitant penalty is exacted by the marine insurance people. At one time this rate was as high as ten times the figure charged for St. Lawrence bound vessels. This is bad enough, but even worse than this is the fact that no insured ships may enter the bay after the season, and the length of season is arbitrarily set without regard to the actual safety of the route. Thus you may understand that by the manipulation of insurance rates those people who think they have more to gain by having grain shipped from eastern ports can prevent the use of this new route.
I am not blaming them for that. Possibly they have interests tied up, money invested. Nevertheless we feel that it ought to be the policy of the government to make a little more use of the seaport which lies just north of the prairie provinces.
Now I wish to deal for a few minutes with navigation in Hudson bay. First I think we must realize that Hudson bay itself does not freeze over and it would be possible to keep the port of Churchill open with an ice-breaker. However, it is correct that ice drifts down from Baffin bay and from Davis strait to block the entrance to the strait at times. In the fall, navigation is made dangerous because of the fact that fog hangs over the straits. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this danger can be completely eliminated by the use of radar on ships going to those northern latitudes. Then in connection with navigation it has been said that the magnetic compass has too
much deviation in those northern areas to be much good as far as navigation is concerned.
I submit that this government can overcome that difficulty quite readily in this way. I understand that we have about a hundred corvettes that have been decommissioned and are to be destroyed. Practically all these corvettes are equipped with gyro compasses, and there is no reason at all why the government should not have those gyro compasses salvaged and placed on ocean-going ships going into Hudson bay.
In addition, I think we should investigate the possibility of constructing ships suitable for trade in Hudson Bay, just as the Russians have constructed ships suitable for trade in their northern latitudes. In this regard there is something else which I think should be mentioned in connection with Russia's develop- . ment of navigation over the top of the world, over the top of Siberia. Annually the Russians send millions of tons of shipping from European Russia through the Arctic ocean almost to 70 degrees latitude, where it turns south and comes down to Vladivostok, on the Asiatic side of the Pacific ocean. That is done during two months of the summer. Hudson bay is much further south than the Arctic ocean north of Siberia, and I venture to say we could make Churchill, Manitoba, at least an eight month port.
I have just one further word to add in connection with this matter, and that is in regard to the future of northern Canada. I have mentioned already that we must do something in the near future to develop our north country. The Russians are developing their northland, and I should like to see Canada at least keep abreast of them. There is no reason at all why we cannot do in our northern country what they have been doing in theirs. I understand the government have a policy with respect to this route, and I am anxious to hear that policy, because I am sure there are in the present administration men who fully realize the great importance of northern Canada to the future of this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the motion of the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Moore), and I am proud to follow such a gallant sailor as the hon. gentleman has demonstrated himself to be through his service with our own Canadian navy during the war now ended. We are fortunate to have in the House of Commons men who are conversant with sailing and who have a knowledge of shipping, such as the

Port oj Churchill
hon. member. I have a warm feeling for the port of Churchill, and anything I can say or do to bring about a greater use of that port I am going to say and do. Many times I have addressed clubs of one kind and another across Ontario in an endeavour to create an interest on the part of this province in western problems. I believe the greater interest Ontario takes in the west and the problems of the west the better it will be for western Canada, because down here is the place where most of the support has to come from. On the other hand I am delighted to see western members discussing their own problems, and one of them is the port of Churchill.
I rather like to call Churchill the back door of Canada, which indeed it is. We have fine ports on the Atlantic seaboard, on the great river St. Lawrence and on the western coast, and there is no reason why we should not have a port on our northern seaboard as well. Last year I made a trip right down to the Arctic ocean to inquire into the possibilities of shipping from Aklavik on the north shore of our country, and a few years ago I made a thorough survey of the Hudson Bay railway right down to the port of Churchill, so when I speak about Churchill I am speaking about something I have myself examined into and seen.
The southern terminus of the Hudson Bay railway is the Pas. This does not mean "pass" in the ordinary sense; it is called after the Pasquia river, which flow's into the Saskatchewan river near this fine thriving town. It means in Cree "the joining of the waters." From that point to Churchill is a distance of about 506 miles; and this is a mighty fine railway. Whoever had to do with the construction of that line built a spendid roadbed on which to lay the rails, which are of heavy weight capable of carrying an enormous traffic. This was demonstrated very clearly during the recent war when our American cousins shipped a vast number of tons of heavy freight to Churchill for their works in that area. So much was this the case that I believe in 1943. the year of greatest traffic, the road paid a profit of $112,000, of course on operating expenses only. That is a clear demonstration that if the road could obtain the freight, this country would not have to meet annual deficits which, using arbitrary' but fairly correct figures, run from $250,000 to perhaps $550,000 for operating costs alone. In my judgment that is not a heavy deficit, but there is no reason why we should have any deficit whatever.
At the port itself unquestionably Canada possesses one of the largest and certainly' one of the best built elevators in the world. This elevator was constructed at that remote northern location by a member of this House of Commons, an engineer of note, none other than the present Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe). One thing I like about the minister is that he does know a great deal about construction, and that elevator at Churchill is a tribute not only to those who planned it but to those who built it. I have not seen a better elevator anywhere, and I have seen a great many of them. The sad thing about it is that the elevator is not used to anything like the extent it should be. I believe from 1931 to 1945 the total amount of wheat shipped over that road was only' something like 24.000,000 bushels. The maximum use was back in 1932, I believe, when the road carried something less than 5.500.000 bushels of wheat. The capacity is a great deal more than that, and that capacity should be used.
I should like to see some new policy in connection with the operation of the Hudson Bay railway, Mr. Speaker, under which we could arrange to deliver over that route all that it could handle and ship. The shipping capacity is perhaps not as great as some would think, though it may' be greater than will be admitted by those who have not been using the shipping facilities to their limit. The general opinion is that the port is good for a maximum of about four months a. year. This might be lengthened, of course, through the use of ice-breakers, to break up the very heavy off-shore ice formations, and to break up the ice in the bay itself. Ice comes down from the north toward the south end of the bay', and shipping using the port late in the season and entering Hudson bay' itself would have to sail south and out around great sheets of ice. If those sheets were broken up by ice-breakers such as are in operation at Petsamo in northern Finland-at present owned by Russia-or at Archangel, the port might be kept open to some such time as was mentioned by the hon. member who introduced the resolution.
I do not feel competent to say how long the port should be kept open, but I am satisfied we could use it to the greatest advantage for between three and four months a y'ear. If we did that we would be able to ship not less than 15 million to 20 million bushels of wheat in a season. The elevator capacity' is sufficient, running in the neighbourhood- of about three million bushels or more. I believe there is that much in it at the present time. So that throughout a shipping season, if w'e started
Port of Churchill

out with a full elevator it would be an easy matter to handle between 15 to 20 million bushels of wheat a year. That operation would save the country an annual deficit both on capital and in operating costs. It seems to me that in all the years I have been in the house capital and interest charges have run as high as So million or $6 million a year- although I do not remember the exact figure.
If fifteen to twenty million bushels of wheat were shipped over that route in a year-and more should be shipped, if possible-the operations would save the country an annual deficit, and would seem to me to be amply justified, and the procedure which would be dictated by ordinary common business sense. In addition to that, through constant use of the route during the shipping season and the natural increase in knowledge acquired by those sailors and by those associated with shipping who would use the route, the length of time during which it could be used would undoubtedly increase. In any event I maintain it should be used.
While I had not expected this resolution would be reached to-day and, as a result, have not my notes before me, my memory is that the three western provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, backed with their crown lands the money that was invested in the building of the route, $50,000,000. At that time, when the construction of the route was proposed, the federal government did not feel inclined to advance the required sum of money, and it was for that reason that the provinces gave this guarantee, in order that the country might be opened up. For that reason those prairie provinces are keenly interested in the use of the route and, in my judgment, a greater use of it would open up new trade channels.
As the previous speaker has said, it is much shorter by rail and sea from Saskatoon or other western Canada points to the European market than it is from Chicago to that market. The water route is longer, but of course it is cheaper. The rail route from Saskatoon, or from Manitoba elevator points, down to the bay, is much shorter.
This applies not only to the shipping of wheat. I remember well having seen fine cattle pens up there, and having listened to the men at the port tell how they were able to ship cattle, and I remember their statement that the cattle arrived overseas in first-class condition. I see no reason why a number of ships could not carry cattle and other farm stock from that port to the old country, thereby putting more money into the pockets of the western farmers.
I am one who believes that the more money we leave in western Canada or with western farmers the better it will be for eastern Canada. People have said to me, "What business is it of yours whether the west develops or not?" Well, it is every man's business; it is the business of every easterner, and particularly if he is engaged in business. If he is neither manufacturing nor in production, he may not be so keenly interested. I was in my time in the manufacturing class, and naturally the advancement of the west meant a great deal to the business in which I was engaged. The greater the amount of money that is put into the pockets of western farmers, the more they will buy; the more they buy, the more men are given employment in Ontario and Quebec and other eastern provinces.
Cattle and wheat could be sent over that route. I have examined it carefully. I know that not less than 250 of the 500 miles is fairly good timber country, good fishing country, and not altogether improvident agricultural country. I have seen crops of every description in the area, and I have no doubt that if the roadway were used to a greater extent, so that all the little towns and villages along its route would have more to do and more men employed, greater and greater trade would be built up. Certainly large quantities of timber could be shipped from the area.
I do not know who would be responsible for the improvement of the Pas. It is situated at a natural trade crossing on the Saskatchewan river. That river would be a great trade artery, if used - and it is not, although I hope it will be some day. I hope the time is. not far distant when it may be a shipping route of note. However the fact is that, east and west of the Pas little has been done to develop trade. There is no railway east or west, only to the north-nothing but the river itself. Then, the equipment on the river is not what it should be. One reason for the lack of development is that the docks are a disgrace to that part of the country. I have no doubt the Minister of Reconstruction is familiar with them. Those docks are built on the Pasquia river, and they are a menace to life. To enter a boat at The Pas to go either east or west on the river-and those boats are small-one almost takes his life in his hands. The docks are indeed in a dilapidated and dangerous condition.
I believe the whole country could be built up and traffic developed for the railway if an

Port of Churchill
honest effort were made to open, up the country east and west of the town of The Pas, which has a population of 5,000 to 8,000. One must be careful in making an estimate of the size of a town; if it is too high, it is ridiculous, and if it is too low, the townspeople are offended. However, my leader would know more about that, because he represented the area for some time in the local legislature. Perhaps if I said the population is around
5,000	or 6,000 I would not be far out.

subtopic: ENCOURAGEMENT OF USE OF HARBOUR AND PORT FACILITIES
speechtext:
People moved in there with high hopes. If The Pas had half a chance and was backed up as it should be, it would soon become an important distributing centre. If given a chance, there is no reason why it should not equal the size of that fine city of Prince Albert or, better still, become something like Edmonton.
The north area is undoubtedly one of the best mineral areas in the world. I do not know of any place where so much mineral wealth is concentrated in such a small area as that around Flin Flon and Sherritt Gordon. There are a score of new mines opening up along the Hudson Bay railway and along the old canoe route from the Pas to Churchill. That district is fine minerally and not too bad agriculturally, particularly the southern end. There is not a great deal of timber, but there is sufficient to meet the requirements of the country. There is a splendid road bed, an excellent elevator, and the best equipment of the Canadian National rolls down to that port.
I am going to ask the minister in charge when preparing his estimates for next year- I imagine it is too late to do anything this year, because by this time probably everything is frozen-to make arrangements to use that route to a much greater extent. We should arrange to ship fifteen to twenty million bushels of wheat over that route next year to start with. I discussed this matter with wheat importers in Liverpool, and at Birkenhead with cattle importers, and I was told that this route has great merit. So far the route has been more damned than praised, but I am always going to praise it until it is used more than it is to-day.
I do not know that there is a great deal more I can say. I have a warm feeling for that whole country. The power possibilities are tremendous. The railroad passes by two of the most marvellous power sites in Canada, the Kettle and the Manitou rapids. The banks are solid rock and the dams could be built as high as one wanted them. I may
be exaggerating, but I believe that these sites are capable of producing from two to two and a half million horsepower each. I am thinking of the possible height of the dams that could be built and the reservoirs that could be built up behind them, running back almost to lake Winnipeg. In fact, the lakes almost join together and between is what might be called a river So that there is vast power there. Long before you come to Manitou or Kettle rapids there is an excellent power site at White Mud rapids where a vast amount of power could be developed. So, Mr. Speaker, that territory has a great wealth of natural resources. The only route into it by rail is the Hudson Bay railway. The more we use the Hudson bay route for shipping across the sea, the more the Hudson Bay railway will be used; the more that railway is used, the greater the number of the people who will go into that country the more the country will be opened up, and the more it is opened up the greater the volume of business that will come down to Davenport riding and elsewhere. I have to think of Davenport riding, sir, because it has I know many manufacturing plants of every description.

As my hon. freind says, one of the better ridings. I have never yet said that it is the best riding, because I think if I did Mr. Deputy Speaker, who is occupying the chair at the moment, would say "next to Brantford". But it is a wonderful riding so far as the working men in it and industry are concerned. I have never asked for anything for my riding in this house. I have never even asked for a post office. I have asked for nothing for my riding except jobs for the workmen I represent, and there are from forty to forty-five thousand of them working in plants and factories in my riding. I can see no way of getting jobs for them unless the companies that employ them get orders, and I know of no better way of getting orders for those companies than by opening up and developing this country. I will strongly support the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) or the Minister of Transport, whichever minister is responsible, in doing every thing he can in bringing about a greater use of the Hudson Bay railway and of the magnificent port of Churchill.
I shall not take time to speak of the history and the great many advantages of that port. It has a depth of thirty-five feet of water right at the docks, and modern equipment has been installed for the unloading of wheat cars.
10S4
Port of Churchill

Four cars of wheat can be unloaded on each side at the one time, approximately, 40,000 bushels of grain or more an hour, and grain can be loaded into two ships at the same time at the rate of 150,000 bushels to 160.000 bushels an hour. These are great port facilities-too splendid to have them standing idle, particularly when our western elevators are filled with wheat and are crying out for the wheat to be put on trains and shipped to Europe.
I cannot see how the opening up of the Hudson Bay railway and the port of Churchill would be anything but of great benefit to western Canada, and whatever is of great benefit to western Canada, whatever puts more money into the pockets of the farmers and business men of western Canada, means in the last analysis more orders for the factories in the riding of Brantford. Mr. Deputy Speaker, more orders for the factories in Davenport riding-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) has won the name of parliament's ambassador of good will. It has been his good fortune to travel perhaps more extensively in Canada than any other member of parliament. He has invariably found it possible in the course of his travels to become familiar with the problems of the people living in those areas, and upon returning to parliament he has always come to the defence of those who live in remote places and puts in a word, as he has to-day, for greater consideration for the frontiers of Canada.
Having gone to public and high school in this province perhaps I might be forgiven for saying that a great many people here think that the most important part of the world is confined within the boundaries of Ontario. In view of the fact that there are 147 members in the House of Commons from Ontario and Quebec and 98 from all other parts of Canada, it is only natural that those of us who represent constituencies outside these two provinces should find it necessary from time

to time to bring to the attention of the government and the house the problems of other parts of the country as we see them.
I would remind the house that two years after Champlain founded the city of Quebec, Henry Hudson left Great Britain with the Discovery in quest of a new and shorter route to Japan and China and the far east. He left on April 17, and two months later his party had reached Iceland. There they managed to gather some wild fowl to replenish their diminishing larder. On July 5, they reached the east coast of Ungava. By the 19th of July they had passed Cape Hope's Advance, and the optimism of Hudson was marked by the name he gave to that point. Then after zigzagging back and forth for five months hoping to find an opening that would lead to the far east, he was eventually disappointed and was forced to winter in the southwest comer of James bay. Hudson's journal indicates that on the 10th of November his ship was frozen in. Later in the year one of the Indians in the region came and looked for the first time upon these strange white faces with their long beards, and he was sent away feeling very happy, carrying with him a knife and a looking glass and some buttons, the gift of Hudson. He returned the following day with two beaver skins, which he gave to Hudson to express his appreciation of his kindness the previous day. He also had two deer skins with him, which were exchanged for a hatchet, and so during these winter months of 1610-11 the first trading took place up in the far north.
The records tell us that the crew had a very difficult winter, and some of its members became most unruly. When they finally set out in the spring, Hudson, his young son and seven of the sick men were cast adrift in the ship's boat. The carpenter offered to join Hudson if his tool chest were given to him. The other members of the crew were glad to have one mouth less to feed and gave the carpenter his chest, and the carpenter then joined Hudson and his companions. What happened to them is one of the unsolved mysteries of the north. No one has ever been able to guess what happened to Hudson and his small company. But the Discovery, with the other members of the crew, reached Digges Island later in the spring. Three men went ashore to see if the Eskimos there would not give them some supplies to tide them over, and the three of them were killed by the Eskimos. The mate. Juet, who was chiefly responsible for plotting against Hudson, died of starvation while crossing the Atlantic, and only four out of the original twenty-three reached Plymouth in the following summer.
It would be impossible for me in the time at my disposal to go into the fascinating

Port of Churchill
history of this great north country but mention should be made of the founder of Churchill, Jens Munck. In 1619, as the commander of the Unicom and Lamprey, he set out to find the Northwest passage. The ships were fitted out by the king. They reached Churchill and spent the winter there. They had a very difficult time. They were short of food all through the winter, and on the 6th of May, 1619. Munck wrote in his journal:
The bodies of the dead He uncovered because none of us had strength to bury them.
By June, Munck and two of his crew were all that was left. The grass was beginning to sprout; two of the sailors crawled ashore and collected some of the grass and sea nettles, and this vegetable diet seems to have checked their disease. They returned to their ship and succeeded in restoring to health their commander, who had said "Good night to all the world" and commended his soul to God. as he did not think there was any chance of coming home alive. However, the two sailors and Munck out of the crew of sixty-four reached Norway in September, 1620, on the Lamprey.
As I said, I have not the time to go into the history of the Hudson Bay railway and the port of Churchill. The hon. member for Davenport and the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Moore) have dealt with certain aspects of the matter. There is no doubt at all that the people of Canada have a very large investment in the Hudson Bay railway and in port facilities, and that the route provides a feasible means of transportation between the prairie provinces and Great Britain.
I have on my desk a number of reports of the imperial shipping committee. I shall quote from the General Report in 1930 signed by H. J. Mackinder, Chairman. The committee comprised representatives of the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, South Africa and India, two shipowners, one shipbuilder, one manufacturer and a merchant. The report was signed at London on May 23, 1930. I quote from the summary of its recommendations :
For two hundred years the Hudson's Bay Company has transported its cargoes to and from Europe by the Hudson Bay route. For probably one hundred and fifty years of this period these cargoes were successfully carried in .sailing ships, consequently it does not seem unreasonable to suppose that modern ships, modern equipment and modern ideas should meet with a considerably greater degree of success, and that a very great and important route will eventually be developed, provided always that in the initial stages of the development every precaution is taken to provide for the protection of the vessels using it.
Then there were certain recommendations regarding charting, aids to navigation, icebreakers and fuel bases. I think it must be said to the credit of the departments con. cerned here that the recommendations regarding aids to navigation and so forth have been carried out to a very considerable extent.
In 1939, on July 19, just before the war broke out, another report was made by the imperial shipping committee. I should like to quote a few sections from the report:
13. There have been during the nine seasons since the route was opened 64 voyages to Churchill, and in our opinion the stage of development may now be considered as over. The way is adequately charted and equipped with the usual aids to navigation, and the exceptional circumstances on account of which the warranty is imposed-ice. fog and magnetic disturbance-are known and have been provided against by the gyro compass, direction finding by radio and the very efficient services of the Canadian patrol vessels. With the sole exception, therefore, of the difficulty which might arise of securing adequate salvage if a vessel should be wrecked late in the season, it is the view of the committee that the Hudson Bay route need not be considered as more risky than the St. Lawrence.
14.	The Underwriter's representatives have agreed to regard the past nine seasons as dosing the dewiopment period of the route, the casualties which have occurred being regarded as paid for by the premiums received. It is clear, however, that before any substantial reduction in the rate of premium for suspending the warranty to Churchill can be secured, an increased number of voyages to and from Churchill will be necessary. There are at present (July. 1939) approximately eight cargoes of wheat in the elevator at Churchill available for shipment when the season opens, and if there is a fairly good harvest this year, it should be practicable to set up a new record in the number of voyages in the season.
15.	In view of the very small number of cargoes available for transport from Churchill in 1937 and 1938, the Joint Hull Committee have not been able to see their way to recommend to the Underwriters a further reduction in the premium for suspending the -warranty for the coming season 1939 and the rates to be charged will be the same as in 1938. But in consultation with our Chairman, the Joint Hull Committee have taken note of the fact that there are already at Churchill for shipment from the 1938 season's crop some eight cargoes of wheat, and they have agreed that if some twenty cargoes in all are brought away from Churchill in 1939 and no serious loss occurs, they -will be prepared to give favourable consideration to the question of recommending a further reduction in 1940 from the rates of premium chargeable in 1939.
During the shipping season of 1939 war broke out and it was not possible to have the twenty vessels move through Churchill as was suggested.
I hold in my hand a memorandum written by D. J. Munro, CjM.G., a captain of the royal navy, and also a nautical assessor for the courts of Scotland. He made a careful study of the possibilities of the northern
Port of Churchill

routes. Hon. members might be interested in some of his remarks regarding Hudson bay and strait. This is what he says:
The safe navigation of Hudson straits is now greatly aided by four instruments perfected during the last few years, via:
(1)	Echo depth recording
(2)	Wireless direction-finding stations
(3)	Gyroscopic compass
(4)	Radar. An instrument which enables dangers invisible by reason of darkness, fog, snow, rain, etc., to be indicated to the mariner, especially icebergs and land.
In comparing the hazards of this route with the hazards of routes in other parts of the world he mentions that commercial ships have now gone from Murmansk to Vladivostok. This is what he said:
Commercial ships have now gone from Murmansk to Vladivostok. In 1935 two ships left Murmansk and two left Vladivistok carrying 9,000 tons of freight between them. The Vancetti and Iskra arrived at the latter port on 11th September-the Anadr and Stalingrade entered Murmansk on 11th and loth of September. These craft carried supplies for ports established at the mouths of the great rivers Ob, Yenisie, and Lena. The distance was over 3,000 miles, and they had not the latest up-to-date instruments to aid them. The Russians have kept their war performances on this route much to themselves, but there are various substantiated reports of submarines arriving by this route at Vladivostok.
The hon. member for Churchill pointed out, and I think rightly so, that on the ships that are now being decommissioned there is a valuable equipment that might be made available on the Bay route.
With regard to the hazards, I think we should not lose sight of the fact that there are hazards in sailing the St. Lawrence route. I crossed to Great Britain on a cattle boat one summer. We left Quebec city in June. We rode at anchor for some three days in the Newfoundland area. There were ice hazards nearby; we were in dense fog. It has never been suggested that the St. Lawrence route should be discontinued because of those hazards. The evidence that is available clearly indicates that the port of Churchill and Hudson strait can be navigated successfully, and many of us feel that it can navigated for a much longer period than has hitherto been accepted by government authority.
As the hon. member for Davenport pointed out, it is important to western agriculture that its products be placed on world markets with the costs reduced to a minimum. I hold in my hand one of the booklets put out a number of years ago by the "On to the Bay" association which made an intensive study of freight rates. They give the distances betwen various

centres in western Canada and Liverpool via Churchill and Montreal. According to the rates which apparently prevailed in 1931, when this report was written, on a carload of live stock being shipped from Yorkton, Saskatchewan, to the old country, there would be a saving of $102; on butter and dressed poultry from Yorkton there would be a saving of $300; on eggs in carload lots there would be a saving of $134 and some cents.
I have here one of the reports of the board of grain commissioners for Canada dealing with the movement of grain. This report was presented with the compliments of the secretary, Mr. John Rayner, dated Fort William, Ontario, March, 1939. It gives the charges in connection with handling at country elevators, railway freight to Churchill, actual handling at Churchill, ocean freight rates and marine insurance approximate average transportation handling charges per bushel of wheat between the producer in western Canada and the arrival of the vessel at British ports, first by way of Churchill and then by way of Vancouver and Montreal. The Churchill rates as given here are 29-25 cents per bushel; Vancouver rate is 35-25 cents, and the Montreal rate by way of the great lakes, 35-25 cents.
It will be readily appreciated that these substantial savings in the getting of agricultural products from western Canada to the European buyer in the shortest possible time and at the lowest cost will be important factors in determining how much trade we are likely to have in the post-war period.
It is true that the people of Canada have spent considerable sums of money in this development, but I wish to suggest that it must never be regarded as an unwise expenditure. I might remind the house that we make very large appropriations for Montreal, Vancouver and Halifax. I hold in my hand a sessional paper which was brought down in 1940 in reply to a question of mine asking for the total amounts paid by parliament to Montreal between the years 1935 to 1939. In those years we appropriated for Montreal $7,000,000 and some odd; Churchill $926,000 and some odd; Vancouver $2,234,000 and some odd, and Halifax $4,954,000 and some odd. I am not complaining about these expenditures. I think it is important that the government vote money to see that the facilities at Halifax, Vancouver and Montreal are maintained in an efficient state.

May I ask the hon. member a question? Are the figures he gave capital expenditures?

Port oj Churchill

The questions were as follows:
1.	How much was spent by the dominion government for dredging the St. Lawrence river and Montreal harbour, and for operating and administering the St. Lawrence ship channel during the years from 1935 to 1939?
2.	How much was spent during the years 1935 to 1939 under the Maritime Freight Rates Act to compensate railways for the difference between the tariff tolls and normal tolls on all traffic moved during the above mentioned years?
3.	How much was spent during the years 1935 to 1939 to provide for construction and improvements in connection with the Hudson Bay Railway, and to provide for losses in connection with the operation of the railway during the above years?
4.	How much money was advanced by the dominion government during the years 1935 to 1939 for the following: (a) Montreal harbour; fb) Churchill harbour; (c) Vancouver harbour;
(d)	Halifax harbour?
I have a table which I should be pleased to place on Hansard with the permission of the house.
It is already on. Mr. MacKINNON: Is it already on?
So far as Halifax is concerned, they were capital expenditures, not dredging.

As pointed out by one of the other speakers this afternoon, in 1908 prairie lands were definitely set aside and ear-marked to provide money for the Hudson Bay railway, and lands were sold to the amount of $42 million, of which $20 million was received in cash. I find this information in an address delivered by Mr. J. M. Stevenson, of the "On to the Bay" association, at its annual meeting in Saskatoon on December 7, 1940. This is what he said:
But in 1908, prairie lands were definitely set aside and earmarked to provide money for the Hudson Bay railway, and such lands were sold in the form of purchased homesteads and preemptions, resulting in some $42 million, of which $22 million was received in cash. This area, therefore, can reasonably assert that it has paid almost the entire cost, and surely this constitutes a substantial reason why we may justifiably demand that the investment be not allowed to lapse.
The money that has been spent has made possible in the north country developments which have had a far-reaching effect on Canada's economy. If this railway had not been undertaken and built when it was, the very valuable deposits from Flin Flon, for example, would not have been available during these past years of war. I realize that Flin Flon is a long way from Churchill, but after the Hudson Bay railway was started it became possible for prospectors to go into the far north country, and several rich mineral areas have been developed. During the war tihe production of copper, zinc, silver, gold and cadmium by Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting company were important factors in Canada's war effort.
We have also very rich fishing grounds in the north. We have Reindeer lake, Beaver lake and a dozen other fresh water lakes that supply fish to the New York market. We have also very popular and promising tourist grounds. Few members apart from the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) have taken the trouble to visit Canada's great northland in the western provinces. I have been through the Alps; I am familiar with the Lake of the Woods country, the Thousand Island area in the St. Lawrence, and the Mus-koka country; but I have not found any place more beautiful than northern Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Some day these places will be a resort for citizens from the United States who will come north to enjoy the fishing and hunting that are available.
Up in the northern part of my own constituency on the Churchill river we have the Island falls development. The plant supplies

power for Flin Flon and Sherritt Gordon, and more than $8 million has been spent in developing this modern power project. Quite recently an article appeared in the Toronto Daily Star referring to that area as Canada's Shangri-la. All the houses are electrically heated. There are electric lights and various city conveniences. I believe every house has a frigidaire, and I have not found any place in Canada where the standard of living is higher than it is in the small community of Island Falls on the Churchill river.
I admit that this is a considerable distance from Churchill. . Some who have visited Churchill say that they would not like to live in the far north. I think it is very fortunate that the people throughout the world do not all want to live in the same place. We have two daughters going to school in Saskatchewan. They have not been in Ottawa for some time, but they think that Ottawa is the last place in the world to live. In their opinion Canora in Mackenzie is the ideal place.
The last time I went into Churchill I travelled with a mounted policeman and his wife who had been away from the north a year and a half. They had gone down to visit relatives in the New England states and they said, "Thank goodness we do not have to live in New Jersey for the rest of our lives." They were most impatient to get back to the north country.
During the war a good deal of attention was paid to the improvement of this area. Just this afternoon an answer was brought down to a question of mine. I asked: "How much has the Canadian government agreed to pay to the United States for American bases at (a) the Pas; (b) Churchill, Manitoba; (c) Southampton island?" The figures are quite interesting. The amount in connection with the Pas is small, $415,000. We are paying the United States $6,206,800 for their work at Churchill and in connection with Southampton island, $5,318,870.
I was in Churchill while a good many Americans were there. My wife had the misfortune to be taken seriously ill while w^e were in the north and she spent several days in their hospital. She had at her service seven of the best qualified doctors to be found in the United States. They were in northern Canada to look after the health of United States soldiers who were guarding our northland. Needless to say she had the best medical and hospital services possible. Now that the war is over and Canada has agreed to pay $6,200,000 for what has been done at Churchill, I do not think it is unreasonable

Port oj Churchill
to ask that we spend a little more money to give this northern route a chance to prove all that some of us have claimed.
Perhaps we are over-optimistic about the possibilities. The resolution before the house states that in the opinion of the house the government should take into immediate consideration the advisability of encouraging the fullest possible use of the harbour and port facilities at Churchill, Manitoba, or the transferring of the management and control of the said port to a joint board appointed by the governments of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta.
I have before me a proposal that has come from one of the organizations in western Canada. A number of resolutions have come to members of parliament from people in the west who for some reason or other think that Churchill is not getting a square deal. Obviously, a proper management for Churchill required an organization of a different character from that of the board set up to supervise the other ports. The average age of the Saskatchewan or the western farmer, hon. members may be surprised to know, is very high indeed. The young men marched off to the war, in spite of the fact that they were farmers' sons, and boys and girls came east to get war work. Let me ask hon. gentlemen from the east this question: Have they ever considered what it would be like to have their sons and daughters going 2,000 miles to get a job? I wonder how those who come from Quebec would like that? It is an honest fact that if a boy wants a job in industry he has to go at an early age 2,000 miles from his own home and his family influences.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Many people went from the east to the west to get jobs.

I was speaking of industry. That is not a good national situation, and it is one which the development and encouragement of a new route would help to overcome. What I have said may give rise to the idea that some opposition may be raised in central Canada against government encouragement of the Hudson bay route, but I contend that such opposition would be purely selfish and in the long run short-sighted. For fifty years a golden stream of western wheat has flowed down through central Canada. This left a good deal of sediment in its path. It has turned into a stream of gold. When hon. members consider the Icing haul, the discriminatory freight rates, the protective tariff that has been in existence in this country so long, I think they will agree with me that the western wheat lands have contributed their share and more to the upbuilding of this nation.
And now we want from the east and central Canada and Halifax, not large sums of money but a little sympathy and support in the upbuilding of the west; for, as Sir Ashley Cooper, governor of the Hudson's Bay company, said a day or two ago to a western audience:
Your imports will be governed largely by eastern Canada. The question of trade between western Canada and Britain is not so much a
IMr. Knight.]
matter for Canada and Britain to deal with but one to be settled between eastern and western Canada. Great Britain will take all the products of western Canada she can pay for.
But the amount she can pay for will depend a good deal on the amount we in Canada are willing to import from her. I suggest that some of these imports could be profitably brought to the port of Churchill through Hudson bay. There was a good deal of opposition to the building of this road and the equipment of the port. For years the whole thing was a political football, but now we have fait accompli, a transportation system which by 1932 had proved that it would work.
Surely that selfish and petty opposition should now disappear. Surely we have reached the stage when we are prepared to put the public good before the private purse. It is queer, though, how men who will send their sons even cheerfully to war, and with some degree of resignation contemplate the fact that they will not return, will oppose tooth and nail any public scheme which will affect their own pockets.

Before six o'clock I was
speaking in support of the resolution asking for sympathetic consideration and active support on the part of the government for the Hudson bay route. I had shown the importance of the route to my own community; I had discussed its importance from a national point of view, which to my mind is infinitely more important; I had pleaded for it as a means of bringing people and industries to my part of the country and to this nation as a whole, and to the best of my ability I had answered the arguments of the senior hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) in opposition. That attitude of opposition, Mr. Speaker, has done more injury than good to this country. It is the attitude which says, if we cannot have something for ourselves, then let no one else have it. What we need in this country, sir, are kindly hearts, open minds and, above all the vision that tells us that what is good for one is good for all, the vision that will make our country great. Good luck to Halifax as far as I am concerned; long may it prosper. For the hon. member who lives there I have nothing but best wishes and sympathy. I have been there twice. My own view is that it is rather depressing to think that between Halifax

Port of Churchill
harbour and Cape Race lie scattered the ribs of 280 gallant ships which have gone to Davy Jones' locker. I had hoped, nay I was almost convinced that such opposition had ceased. If you are interested in the opposite view I would recommend the reading of "Sea of Destiny" by Dyson Carter. He claims that a deliberate attempt to sabotage the route was made by eastern commercial and transportation interests and marine insurance companies, supported by the press. He even offers the terrible indictment that the sinking of the ship Bright Fan early in the history of the completed route was not altogether accidental. Of course I have no proof in regard to this statement, and he will have to take the responsibility for it himself. I do know there was joy in certain quarters in Montreal when the Bright Fan went down, but that joy was somewhat tempered some two weeks later by the news that the Pennyworth had gone down in a fog off Montreal. The Pennyworth had successfully cleared her cargo from Hudson bay just a short time before.
However that may be, shipping out of Churchill increased until in 1936 some fourteen ships steamed out of the port with
5,000,000 bushels of No. 1 wheat aboard. The Imperial shipping committee, investigating a wreck that occurred that year, declared:
As far as physical risks are concerned we are convinced that the Hudson's bay route is not more dangerous, and in some respects is less dangerous, than the St. Lawrence route.
I said, sir, I had hoped the opposition would cease. I am afraid that, like the poor, propoganda persists in being with us. I have in my hand a little pamphlet which just came to my desk. I do not know who sent it; no one knows. It just came. It did not cost a penny; I was very welcome to it. As a matter of fact, they hope I will read it. Perhaps it was sent to be received in time for this debate. Again, I do not know; but at any rate it is free. It represents this selfish viewpoint, this one-sided idea about which I was talking. It reminds me of certain other pamplets which you will remember were sent around in this country prior to June 11, except that this one is white in colour. It should have had a bit of that red mail-order paint on it to dress it up a little. No one knew who sent those other pamphlets, either; they just came, and we were welcome to them. Hon. gentlemen opposite did not know where they came from; hon. gentlemen to my right did not know where they came from, and they are all honourable men. Let me read a little from this pamphlet, choosing a 47696-70
place almost haphazardly. The writer seems to be interested in railroads; so am I He
says:
We can realize that the C.P.R. made western Canada . . .
Well, that is a good sentence; it reads equally well in reverse. Then he goes on to
say:
Public opinion on the prairies forced the gov- eminent into backing great and even unwise ventures in providing competition for the C.P.R.
Then a little later comes the line that caught my eye; this is my reason for introducing this pamphlet into this debate:
Perhaps one day the line to Hudson bay will be available.
He goes on to speak of other railway ventures and then adds:

Then another line:
. . . and it is now taken for granted that we shall, forever, have two railways in western Canada.
The gentleman looks a long way ahead. He is also interested in tariffs and says:
As a matter of fact, even good free traders are apt to doubt whether a tariff which has been on for any length of time can be taken off completely, and overnight, without making things worse than they were . . . He is also interested in the Winnipeg grain exchange, and say$:
