And he feels very sorry for them.
To get back to the more serious question, although I believe what I have read has some bearing upon it, for a moment I should like to discuss the question of the danger to shipping, which of course is a vital factor in the situation, because the success of this project depends upon getting reasonable rates in marine insurance. Even before the war the dangers of the route, like those of the St. Lawrence, had been progressively mastered by scientific advance, with the installation of gyro compasses, radio direction finders and the employment of icebreakers. During the last war many devices must have been evolved making for the safety of ships at sea, devices which can be applied to the occasional fog and ice conditions encountered in Hudson bay. As some of the previous speakers have said, I imagine

Port oj Churchill

radar holds immense possibilities in this connection and will open a whole new field of navigation.
The other day in this house I asked that the Minister of Transport produce copies of reports furnished by the United States government in regard to a survey made during the last war by that government of meteorological conditions over the route. We were told that 6uch a survey had been made, and I understand that both the waters and the air were thoroughly investigated. I was promised a copy of the report and I know it will reach me in due course. Unfortunately it is not available for this debate. I expect and hope it will contain information encouraging the use of the Hudson bay route. Let me draw one thing to the attention of hon. members. During the war the Americans took no chances on leaving unguarded that great body of open water which leads directly into the heart of this continent. They know the potentialities and the virtues of that great route, and so they took that survey. I am told that the Americans went in there to Hudson bay, to a frozen sea as it has been called by so many people, in the heart of winter. I am not vouching for the truth of that statement, because I was not there; but I am offering it for what it is worth. I hope to get the information from the minister later on.
With all this new information, and with all these new inventions, surely the price of marine insurance will come down. If so, the success of the route will be assured, and the wish of the people in the prairie provinces will be fulfilled. I suggest lo the government that if marine insurance is not cut down proportionately as, in the light of new inventions, it should be, the government should be doing something about it, and should say to the marine insurance companies, you will have to bring your rates down, proportionately, or we will see that there is some other company operating, or some manner in which marine insurance rates may be made reasonable.
The wish that the Hudson bay route be opened was expressed in a recommendation of the United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan branch, to the dominion-provincial conference, in a memorandum of August 4, 1945. May I quote the following from that recommendation:
We recommend action to make full use of the Hudson Bay railway and all facilities at Port Churchill for shipment of products from, and oods to, Canada; that Canadian trade agents e appointed to facilitate trade through the Hudson Bay-Port Churchill route; that Canadian^ trade agents established in other countries be instructed to develop trade through the Hudson Bay-Port Churchill route, and that the project be operated under a board of western management.

This request for a western board, about which some curiosity has been shown here to-day, in conjunction with the governments of the prairie provinces, is also put forth by the Hudson's bay route association, an organization which is leaving no stone unturned to bring about the resumption of traffic over that route. The board's being of that composition would procure action forthwith, I am sure, and would remove any suspicion that may linger in the west that pressure was being brought to hinder operations.
We hope, and have reason to believe, that the government will act upon the idea expressed in this resolution, particularly in respect of the first part of it. In that event the second part would not be necessary. I have in my possession correspondence which shows that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) attempted to find shipping to bring out of Churchill the grain that is held there. A letter from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) states:
The policy of the government in the matter of Churchill is to facilitate the use of ithis port in every way possible.
Good! We will look for action-and not next year when shipping opens up, but now, to prepare for the time when shipping opens up. May I add in passing that this has been one of the great drawbacks in the past. The authorities would wait until the weather was changing, and when ships might have been coming in there it was found that preliminary investigation and preparations had to be made. By the time that was done, the season was over.
The road is built and ready. In fact, it is now in use and it has been paid for out of the proceeds of western lands. There is at the port a fair nucleus of equipment with which to start business, and the government has assured us that the ban on shipping, which they say was a necessity owing to war, is now lifted.
We have hope of support from hon. members in the house. I hold in fny hand an interesting pamphlet, somewhat yellowed with age, for it is dated 1926. This pamphlet deals with the Hudson bay route. May I quote haphazardly from the speech-for that is what it is:
The problem of transportation is the great problem of western Canada . . .
Since we are a democratic country governed by the wishes of the majority, and since all the produce of. western Canada before the opening of the Panama canal had to move eastward, every attempt to open up new trade routes has met with opposition which has often been successful . . .
Nor is the Hudson Bay railway the project of the west. It is national in its interest.

In this fashion the then premier of Saskatchewan, now the federal Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) proceeded to prove his point with earnestness and precision. In an eloquent conclusion he states, prophetically, in the light of recent inventions:
Those seamen . . . will find ways and means to stretch the four month's season set down by tenderfoot engineers into six or more months.

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to make a speech, but I should like to ask a question. The port of Churchill is an unnatural port, when we have two railroads which can deliver the grain to the breadbasket of the world, and to a point where we have the greatest wheat handling facilities found anywhere.
My question is this: Is it possible to heat up the Hudson bay and Baffin strait with atomic power, so as to keep the water free of ice? I would ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) or the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) if there is'any possibility of that.

I want to say something about insurance rates, which is another important feature, whether or not ships can get insurance before they move. Insurance for Churchill can be obtained from August 5 to October 15 only, and on ships going in and passing Cape Chid-ley at the eastern end of Hudson strait on August 5 and can be kept on ships leaving Churchill until October 7 without extra premium. This terminal was transferred to the national harbours board for administration, management and control in 1937, and by 1939 there was in sight the biggest programme of grain shipments from the port of Churchill in its history. At that time fifteen cargo-carrying ships were assigned by various shipping companies to load grain at Churchill for Europe. Nine of them were actually named and before the war it looked as though the port of Churchill was going to enjoy a really busy period. Unfortunately, however, war broke out; after a few cargoes of grain had been shipped, one ship was torpedoed on the way out to Hudson bay and the sailings of the others were cancelled because of the hazards of war. Then followed the long years of war when, although the elevator was filled with grain, nothing moved out until 1942, when between seven and eight hundred thousand bushels were loaded on United States ships and carried to New England ports for United States government account.
Shortly after the close of the German war the Canadian wheat board, the national harbours board, and other Canadian agencies made very strong and persistent efforts to secure ships for Churchill in 1945, but owing to lack of shipping, and the necessary scientific navigational equipment such as gyrocompasses, shipping definitely declined to use the port of Churchill in 1945.
I pause here to say a word about the efforts made by the national harbours board and by the Canadian wheat board to do everything in their power to get shipments of grain to Churchill. As the house knows, during the war and even at this time shipping is controlled by virtue of the united maritime shipping agreement, and is in the hands of the British ministry of transport. Notwithstanding the representations made by both agencies, the national harbours board and the Canadian wheat board, the British ministry of shipping thought there were pertinent reasons why shipping to Churchill should be declined. I should like to give the house some of the reasons why that conclusion was arrived at. They are as follows:
First, the ministry of transport was of the opinion that the hazardous nature of the voyage justified taking into account the possible damage or complete loss of the vessel.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to the statement just given by the minister with respect to the route, but like the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) I am still in doubt where he stands on the matter. He spent about one minute of his time, when he started, saying that the government was in favour of the route but that he himself knew very little of the topography and very little about the circumstances of the route, and then he proceeded for thirty minutes to give facts and figures supplied to him by his officials, w'hich are an absolute condemnation of the route. If the route were given a fair show; if the government would go all out, by means of their trade commissioners in the old country, to see that tonnage was brought into that port as well as going out of it, if they would encourage the cooperatives over there to make shipments through that point, and take action in other ways, there is no doubt that the deficit as far as Port Churchill is concerned could be reduced materially.
The resolution placed on the order paper by the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Moore) states:
That, in the opinion of -this house, the gov-ment should take into immediate consideration the advisability of encouraging the fullest possible use of the harbour and port facilities at Churchill, Manitoba-
That is the first part of it. Then it goes on and suggests that if they fail to do this-
-or the transferring of the management and control of the said port -to a joint board appointed by the governments of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta.
The last part is inserted just in case the government are not prepared to go ahead and see that this port is used to the greatest possible extent. If the government should be prepared to do this, then the second part of the resolution does not become operative at all. For a number of years in western

Port oj Churchill
Canada we have had an organization which, has been particularly interested in this port at Churchill. It was organized back in the 1920's, after the last war, when it seemed that the government of that day were going to abandon the project entirely. It was then called the "On to the Bay" association, and was organized to arouse public opinion in western Canada to the point where the government would be forced to continue the route and develop it for shipments to the old country. The association was successful in this. Fort Nelson, which had proved a failure, was dropped. Lord Palmer, I believe it was, carried on an investigation for a suitable port, and Churchill was chosen; the railroad was continued to that port, and the development of the route continued. To-day this organization is known as the Hudson bay route association, and again it is organizing public opinion in western Canada so that the route will not be dropped after this war as it was after the last war. It is urging that the development be continued, because the new inventions brought out during the war, together with the investigation carried on through the meteorological branches established in the north during the war by the United States forces, have placed a great deal of new information at the disposal of the government, and in western Canada it is felt that this route can and should be used now that the war is over.
This organization suggests that if the government at Ottawa are not prepared to go ahead and do the necessary advertising and, if necessary, charter vessels to come to Churchill, the management of the port-not of the railway-should be turned over to a western organization. They have some definite proposals with respect to the type of organization they would like to see take charge of the port, and those proposals have been set out in a brief they have prepared and submitted to at least all western members. They say:
A change such as is proposed should seem highly desirable to the dominion government. The Hudson Bay railway, the railway's port at Churchill, and the bay route in its entirety, are likely to remain a matter of contention, embarrassing to the dominion government as long as that government remains responsible for the success of the bay route . . .
To the provinces assuming administration of the commercial facilities of the port of Churchill it is suggested that they set up an ordinary joint stock company. A full half of the shares should remain with the government, or governments, and this form of organization allows a simple method for dividing and allocating shares he-tween two or more provinces.
Of the remaining half of the shares, a portion, or all, might be offered to such business organizations as are mentioned previously, to be acquired by actual purchase. Such shares, to
add to their attractiveness, might have priority rights for dividends up to a moderate limit such as five per cent. Capital so raised would provide a working fund; and a cash investment would guarantee the continuing interest of the contributors. With assurance of such interest on the part of practical businessmen, many of ,the minor problems of administration would be removed from the shouldeTs of the provincial governments, to be carried by those whose training fits them to deal best with such problems.
The governments should have a majority of directors. Three might be enough, if one represented business interests.
Title to government-built properties should not pass to a joint stock company. Its rights to use of the Saskatoon and Churchill facilities should be limited to leasehold rights, with provision for cancellation.
In other words, they have definite suggestions to offer in regard to the development of the port and the facilities established there. The minister has said that the government have given sympathetic consideration to the port of Churchill. I want to point out one way at least in which they have failed to do so. If I, as a grower of grain in northeastern Saskatchewan, desire to ship to Port Churchill, the freight rate from my shipping point is eighteen cents per 100 pounds, while the freight rate to Fort William or Port Arthur is twenty-one cents. If I sell a carload of grain to go through Churchill, however, I pay the twenty-one cent freight rate to Fort William, even though my grain goes to Churohill. Therefore I do not reap the benefit of having that port contiguous to my farm in western Canada. The same applies to the whole of northeastern Saskatchewan. If the same consideration were given to the port of Churchill that is given to Fort William, Port Arthur and Vancouver, then those of us who live closer to Churchill would pay only the freight rate to that port, just as the people in Alberta who are closer to Vancouver pay the freight rate to Vancouver, even though their grain may be shipped to Port Arthur. Therefore I say that if the government were prepared to give a fair deal to the port of Churchill they would amend the Canada Grain Act of 1940 in such a way as to put shipments to Churchill on the same basis as shipments to any of the other main exporting ports.
Another way they could help material!}' would be by the extension of the Canadian National railway line which runs from Saskatoon to Carrot River, on to the Pas in Manitoba, to connect with the Hudson Bay railway. This would mean that the haul for . grain from the northern part of Saskatchewan and Alberta would be much shorter. In addition, if this railway were continued from Carrot River to the Pas a large area of very good
Port of Churchill

agricultural land would be opened up. As a matter of fact, this is the largest agricultural area in any part of Saskatchewan remaining uncultivated. It is very good land and would be opened up and developed if the railway were continued from Carrot River through to the Pas.
Those are only two ways in which the present government, if they wished to develop the Port of Churchill, could assist in that matter.
The organization in western Canada known as the Hudson bay route association, is entirely non-political; and I am glad to note that the debate in the house to a great extent has remained non-political. It just so happens that members of this group' represent many of the constituencies which are particularly affected by this matter. Nevertheless, when members from, other political groups represented the same constituencies they, too, spoke in favour of this route.
I have under my hand a speech delivered by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) back in 1926, at which time he strongly recommended to the dominion government that the port be developed for shipments of both outgoing and incoming cargoes. For many years the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) has been a supporter of the Hudson bay route. The former Minister of Mines and Resources in the house, who is now a member of the senate, and represented Churchill for a number of years, was also a strong supporter of this route.
I would ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Ohevrier) to give this matter sympathetic consideration, and not to listen to everything that may have been said by members of his department and staff. He, himself, should go to Churchill, see the position there and judge for himself whether or not this is a feasible route. We in western Canada are never going to be satisfied until it is definitely proven that it is not. I contend that, to date, that has not been proven. As a matter of fact, with modern radar and the new meteorological stations which have been established in the northern areas, we feel quite sure that this route can be used to a far greater extent than it has ever been used in the past.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction) :
speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended taking part in the debate. I always feel that people who are most familiar with the subject under discussion had best not impose their views in a manner that may tend to ruin an exchange of theories.
My association with Churchill dates back to (he middle twenties. I have been there, not
(Mr. Wright.]
only at the end of August or in early September when all the tourists visit there, but also in April. I may say my face is still scarred from a frost-bite I got while walking from the train at Churchill to the nearest bunkhouse; and that was in late April.
There are certain facts in the situation which, I suggest, must be faced, particularly in view of the suggestion that the government has not endeavoured to develop Churchill as a port. June is a lovely month in Churchill; the sun shines day and night; there is no hour of the day or night when one cannot read a newspaper. But at that very time ice stretches as far as the eye can see, and that continues on to the end of June. In early July the Churchill river begins to discharge its ice. The ice breaks up and drifts out in large blocks, blocks of a size that no icebreaker with which I am familiar could be expected to cope.	'
The result is that insurance goes in effect on August 5, and I believe no ship would venture into the port earlier than that date. Those are facts; they are not theories in the mind of any official of the Department of Transport. I can vouch for those facts, personally; and I hope my reputation as an engineer is such that I would not be guilty of stating a fact, of which I had knowledge, without stating it correctly.
The season is closed in the fall by slush ice coming down from the Churchill river. The ice forms in the river and is carried out by the current. It would be an unfortunate boat, indeed, which got caught in that slush ice, because most certainly it would have to remain there during the next winter. It is impossible to manoeuvre.
Therefore the length of the season is pretty well determined. It is a matter of about two and a half months; and it would be an exceptional season, indeed, when navigation would be possible for a full three months.
However, we realize that much can be done in two and a half months. The government is aware of the facts, and it was aware of them when it went there. It did not make only a gesture toward developing the port; it made a magnificent job of developing it. Anyone riding to Churchill on the Hudson Bay railway and viewing the harbour facilities would not accuse the government of not having built the port in the full belief that it would be a valuable asset to Canada.
The railroad is as well built as any similar railroad in Canada. The harbour facilities are first-class. Some 1,200 feet of dock were built, and were well built under great difficulties. A grain elevator having all the facilities to be found in any grain elevator in

Port of Churchill
Canada was built at that port, and was built with the knowledge that the season would be short and that the handling of grain must therefore be rapid. With that in mind four automatic car dumpers were installed there, at a time when car dumpers were a novelty in the grain trade. Loading facilities are exceptionally fast. A boat can be loaded at that port in a day without any difficulty. It was known that boats could not afford to stay long at the port, and ample loading facilities were provided so that boats could be cleared quickly. So much for the port facilities.
As I have said, they were built by a Liberal government, and they were built well. They were built with the intention of making Churchill a port of continuing value to Canada. I know something, too, about the efforts made to send business through that port. I know of the negotiations which went on with British shipping lines. Out of all those negotiations we were able to interest only one shipping -line in sending boats to that port; that was the Dalgleish line. The government did make an earnest endeavour to do business through Churchill, and succeeded in doing a considerable amount of business in each season until war conditions made it impossible to operate.
The fact that no other shipping line would interest itself in the port is an indication to me that the shipping profits on the route could not have been fabulous. I know something of the efforts made to bring down insurance rates. Rates were coming down each year, until a boat was lost in the strait, and the insurance rates zoomed up again. Hon. members will understand that insurance rates are based upon the average experience of the route, and the experience on the route into Churchill has not been good, measured in terms of percentages.
I contend that every effort has been made to make Churchill an asset to Canada. Despite those efforts, however, I think hon. members will agree that up to the present time the movement of grain through Churchill has not increased the price of grain at any country loading points in Canada. There are certain points in northern Saskatchewan and northeastern Alberta which furnish the movement. If the shipping rates could be reduced, that area served would widen. But for the greater part of the west, the movement through Churchill can mean very little in the matter of increasing the price of grain at country points.
There are certain factors that have emerged from the war that will offer opportunity for a more intensive use of the route in future years. We now have a considerable fleet of
ships suitable for trading into Hudson bay. These ships are owned by the government, and it will be at the option of the government whether it wishes to insure them or not. We have operated boats through the war years without insurance, and I presume the government will not hesitate to operate into Churchill without insurance.
There are certain devices that have been developed during the war, such as radar, which make it possible for a ship to detect floating ice and to obtain its own position without the use of a compass. In that way a ship is in a stronger position to undertake ventures into new routes than was the case before the war. All this will be in favour of a real trial to make the Churchill route the success that was hoped for when the facilities were built.
In spite of the short season I think it may be possible to reach the objective of those who developed the route, which was a movement of 20,000,000 bushels of grain in the season. That does not sound much when compared with the movement through Port Arthur and Fort William or through Vancouver, but 20,000,000 bushels is a considerable movement for any port. Few ports on the continent have larger movements than that. Therefore I am not suggesting that the outlook for Churchill is hopeless; far from it. I feel that in post-war years the port will develop as far as its physical limitations will permit, and I can assure the house that the government will make every effort to see that that development is pressed actively and vigorously.
As far as the "On to the Bay" association is concerned, I think the government has accepted all the practical representaitons which that body has made. It was suggested at one time that the government should employ an active agent who would be located in the western provinces and who would seek for imports into Canada. I recall that for some years the government employed one of the officers of the Saskatchewan government to perform that duty. The grain office for the port was located in Winnipeg, and a competent officer of the board of grain commissioners was given the exclusive duty of developing grain business to move through Churchill.
I hardly think the latter part of the resolution is a practical suggestion. I can assure my hon. friend that if he believes that is the best way to develop Churchill, and he can find a responsible group who wish to lease the facilities of Churchill on a basis of $1 a year, I will do my best to influence my colleagues to accept the proposal. In saying
mo

that, I am mindful of the fact that it is an expensive port to operate. There are no year-round residents at Churchill. All operators must be moved in at the beginning of the season; they must be gathered up all over the prairies and moved to the port. While the power plant is maintained in operating condition during the winter, the real crew must be moved in in the spring. The crew for the grain elevator must be moved in. All supplies must be moved in, as well as all coal to bunker ships.
And all the water drained out of the mains.

maintopic: ST. MARY RIVER PROPOSED CONSTRUCTION OF RESERVOIR
ST. MARY RIVER PROPOSED CONSTRUCTION OF RESERVOIR
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into immediate consideration the advisability of proceeding with the construction of the St. Mary river reservoir, the key structure of the Lethbridge southeast water conservation project in southern Alberta.
He said. May I give the house somewhat of the background of this resolution. There are in southern Alberta wide areas of land rich and easy to work, relatively near to railways and schools; lands most of which have already been settled and brought under cultivation. But the rainfall in that area is scanty. Crop failure is far too common. The climate is well adapted to the production of field crops of various kinds, including sugar beets, canning crops like peas, beans, corn and tomatoes and all manner of vegetables that grow in moderate climates, alfalfa and grains. As a result of all this, the area is one of great productive potentiality. It would be possible to make that particular region one of the finest sources of food in the
dominion and perhaps on the North American continent. But it requires more water.
There are in the Lethbridge district four major irrigation projects; Lethbridge, Coal-dale, Raymond, Magrath and Taber, comprising in all 120,000 acres. All of this land is irrigated from the St. Mary river through a canal which was constructed early in this century, about 1901 or 1902, by what was known at that time as the A.R. and I., or the Albert Railway and Irrigation company. In most years there is too little water for the area which has been brought under irrigation, so that in the months of July, August and September there is frequently such a scarcity of water that great loss results. Sometimes the scarcity is most acute. Especially is this so when the snow supply, which ordinarily is found in the Rocky mountains, is melted away for one reason or another, thereby causing the water in the river to be low. Sometimes the shortage will be forty per cent, at least, below what it ought to be.
It happens that in the system which they are using there is no reservoir. Water has to be taken out of the river just as the river runs, and consequently when the ri%rer is low the water supply is also low.
There is considerable water available in Alberta, enough of it to turn great stretches of semi-arid land into verdant blooming garden land. There are four international rivers in my constituency flowing through southwestern Alberta: Waterton river, Belly river, the St. Mary river and the Milk river. From these rivers there is available for the project which we are discussing to-night, namely, the Lethbridge southeast water conservation project, a total of 795,7.00 acre feet of water. This quantity, allowing for wastages through evaporation, seepage and the like would be sufficient to supply 465,000 acres of land.
To the waters of the St. Mary river and

the Milk river the United States has a considerable claim. This is how it came about. The two rivers rise, of course, in the United States, but the United States made no serious claims to the waters of these rivers, so far as I know, until back in 1901 when the Alberta Railway and Irrigation company began to build the canal from which Magrath, Raymond and Lethbridge are now watered. Then the United States people began to be concerned; a reclamation act was passed by congress in 1902, and the St. Mary and Milk river project in Montana was authorized in 1903. There then arose protests of citizens on both sides of the line, each thinking that the other nation was getting too much water.
St. Mary River-Reservoir

I should like now to read from the recommendations of the committee, as they are found at page 8:
The construction of the main reservoirs and connecting canals would provide the necessary facilities to store in Canada, Canada's share of these international waters and would thereby be an insurance against the loss of a valuable resource.
Near the bottom of the same page I read as follows:
That the dominion undertake and assume as a 100 per cent responsibility the construction of the main reservoirs and connecting canals to provide storage facilities for Canada's share of the waters of the St. Mary and Milk rivers as apportioned under the order of the international joint commission of October 4, 1921.
Again on page nine:
That the dominion's part in the construction of the project be carried out as a federal postwar development, and that the cost thereof be . regarded as non-recoverable.
I believe the material which I have given is such as to justify the house in passing this resolution, which reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into immediate consideration the advisability of proceeding with the construction of the St. Mary river reservoir, the key structure of the Lethbridge southeast water conservation project in southern Alberta.

maintopic: ST. MARY RIVER PROPOSED CONSTRUCTION OF RESERVOIR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore). I am happy to see the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) in his seat because, if anything is done in connection with the St. Mary river project, it will be done under his department. I am going to direct my remarks principally to him and I know the other members of the house will not mind. After all, it is always good politics and good business to talk to the man who has to do.
If you convince the man who has to do, then you have the job half done.
To advocate irrigation for southern Alberta should not be a difficult job, nor should it be particularly hard to convince anyone who knows anything about the problem of southern Alberta. It is a great problem. I intend to go a little outside the resolution and be more general than the resolution. I do not believe the Minister of Reconstruction can separate this one project from another project which is equally important. They should both be carried on at the same time. The irrigation of southern Alberta is a vital problem. It is of vast importance to Canada. Much of the business built up in eastern Canada, in your own city, Mr. Speaker, and in many other cities in eastern Canada;

many of the plants in your city and in my city-if I were dealing with my own riding I could speak most forcibly-have been expanded because of what little irrigation-it is not little, except when compared with what has been done south of the line-has been done in southern Alberta.
I shall first confine my remarks to the resolution which asks for the construction of a reservoir on the St. Mary river. The -previous speaker has already told the house that four rivers flow into Canada from the United States, all starting in the same glaciers south of Waterton park. The three westerly rivers are the Waterton, the Belly and the St. Mary, and these are the most important to Canada, more so than the Milk river.
I shall say a word about the Milk river and then leave it out from the rest of my argument. The Milk river enters Canada and after flowing through Canada for about 150 miles, or about 125 miles in a straight line, it returns to the United States. The water in that river is all United States water except for the water of some small tributaries that flow in in southern Alberta and southern Saskatchewan. None of these Canadian tributaries has water of any great volume. In my opinion the duty of Canada is to proceed with that which will mean the most to Canada, namely, the St. Mary river project.
On the St. Mary river, about ten miles more or less north of the beautiful little town of Cardston, there is an. excellent site for a reservoir. I do not like to make any comment about engineering problems without knowing something about the matter, and I have visited this site. The banks are quite high and the engineers who were with me said that they could build a dam 150 feet high. They showed me where they had drilled to find foundation sites. If that could be done they could store in that reservoir about 270,000 acre feet of water. What is an acre foot of water? It means the water sufficient to cover one acre of land one foot deep. To convert
270,000	acre feet into cubic feet you would have to multiply 270,000 by 43,560, which is the number of square feet in an acre. In other words, this would be a vast volume of water.
But it is not sufficient to take care of the land which is irrigable but which is not now irrigated in southern Alberta south of the main line of the South Saskatchewan river. More reservoirs would have ter be built. Besides the Spring Coulee reservoir north of Cardston, to which I have just referred, other reservoirs could be built southeast of Lethbridge, one at Chin Coulee, which would be sufficient to conserve 150,000 acre feet, and

St. Mary River-Reservoir
one at Verdigris, good for 140,000 acre feet. There are quite a number of other smaller sites, some of substantial capacity.' The total of all reservoir capacity that could be built south of the South Saskatchewan river- quite apart from the Milk river project which I am not dealing with at the present time- is about 650,000 acre feet. That is more than would be required to take care of the possible acreage which is irrigable but which is not now irrigated, namely, about 345,000 acres. This would take care of all the additional irrigable land south of the main line of the South Saskatchewan river-Old Man river. Old Man river is the principal Saskatchewan tributary in that part of Alberta. As I say, those 345,000 acres could be irrigated by water stored from * the St. Mary river, plus water diverted from the Belly river and sent into the reservoirs just mentioned. The engineering plans are ready for this project. In other words, Canada will have no trouble whatever in finding reservoir capacity in southern Alberta in which to store sufficient water to take care of the
345,000	acres of irrigable land in southern Alberta south of the main line of the Saskatchewan river.	[DOT]
Something was said about the cost of the Spring Coulee reservoir on the St. Mary river. The cost of all the additional reservoirs and irrigation canals in southern Alberta south of the main line of the South Saskatchewan river necessary to store water to irrigate right down to the neighbourhood of Medicine Hat would be around $15,000,000. If that can be done for $15,000,000, the Minister of Reconstruction would receive the support of this whole country. There is not a question of doubt in my mind as to the wisdom of entering into agreements and contracts for the building of irrigation works south of the main line of the south Saskatchewan river. I do not mean that Canada should pay for that, nor do I think the province of Alberta would expect to pay for it, nor do I think the people of southern Alberta would expect Canada to pay for it. But they are not in a position to do it themselves. Therefore the money required to construct these works would have to be guaranteed by the dominion government. It would not in the last analysis cost this country one dollar. Take the Taber area, where the present irrigation canals end just a short distance east of the town, south of the main line of the South Saskatchewan river. From there to Medicine Hat is a fine country, with A-l land, containing all the chemical ingredients required to produce in abundance. That has been clearly demonstrated in the vicinity of Taber itself, where the products produced on irrigated farms are
marvellous. I visited a field where something new not only for that part of the country but for Canada was being produced, namely a field of large cucumbers-I believe they call them dill.

speechtext: Dill pickles.

maintopic: ST. MARY RIVER PROPOSED CONSTRUCTION OF RESERVOIR
speechtext:
Yes. They have recently built in the village of Taber, a thriving village that clearly demonstrates the tremendous business that accrues to any village, town or city in an irrigated area, thirty very large vats, each one capable of containing some twelve tons of large cucumbers. They have also started to grow sweet potatoes in that area and are having success, which goes to show that the land in southern Alberta is A-l, excellent land. All that is required is the water. That district in southern Alberta around Taber would not grow anything of any consequence were it not for the irrigation canals that are there now. In 1943 the precipitation for that area was a little over three inches. You could not grow anything on land with a precipitation of only three inches a year, except perhaps prairie grass, wild sage and rose bush. But with irrigation, see how that area has developed! The same can be done elsewhere. There is just as good land around Raymond and Magrath and Cardston. The whole area in southern Alberta which is now irrigated demonstrates clearly what the land will produce if it has water. If it has water and produces like the one or two examples I have given anyone can readily see that the cost of irrigation works would be liquidated in time.
I am also going to ask for consideration for the territory on the north side of the river, south of the Red Deer area, which I am not going to touch at the moment. I am in favour of irrigating the Red Deer area of Alberta too, but at the moment I confine my remarks to the present irrigation canals north of the main line of the South Saskatchewan river, all of which I have covered very carefully.
The water is taken out of the Bow river on the north side of the main line of the South Saskatchewan river and diverted first to McGregor lake and from there into Little Bow lake. These two lakes have a capacity of 350,000 acre feet of water: In the area, north of the general line of the South Saskatchewan river there are 245,000 additional acres of land which is just as good land as that south of the main line of the South Saskatchewan river, and it should be covered by this general irrigation scheme for southern Alberta. You would have north of the river
245,000	acres, for which there is ample water
St. Mary River-Reservoir

and ample reservoir capacity, not all developed but all of which can easily be developed, and then south of the main line of the river you would have 345,000 acres, or a total of about 600,000 acres in southern Alberta which could be and should be irrigated and for which an ample supply of water is guaranteed, provided that the reservoirs are built, particularly commencing with one at Spring Coulee on the south side of the main line of the river; second, at Chin Coulee; third, at Yerdegris, and fourth, at any' of ten other reservoir sites.
The north side of the river is peculiarly suited right now for the extension of the irrigation system because the main line of irrigation canals are already constructed. The first area to 'be taken in by the new project would be the Retlaw-Lomond area, with which my hon. friends from Alberta are quite familiar. That is an excellent area of land. I have been over it, and I observed that it has an excellent fall which is peculiarly and particularly adapted for irrigation purposes. I am convinced1 that God Almighty in His allwise providence, when He designed that part of Canada and endowed the soil of Alberta with that richness in chemicals which enables it to grow anything, knowing that it did not have the water it requires from precipitation, provided for it to have water, first, by providing the water in the mountains from which the South Saskatchewan river starts, and then by giving a fall to the land for not less than two hundred miles so that the water could flow down without having to be pumped.
The first area, the Retlaw-Lomond area, can easily be taken care of. It is just lying there waiting for the subsidiary canals to be built from the main canal that flows south and east from McGregor lake and from Little Bow lake. The main canal is completed right east to the Bow river, but when it reached the Bow river it stopped, for lack of money. That is to say, the connection of the canal west of the Bow river with the canal east of the Bow river did not take place. The water stops west of the Bow river, but the canal itself is completed east of the Bow river and for another fifty miles in a direct line, but perhaps sixty miles following the circuitous course which the canal takes to within sight of Medicine Hat. If the minister pays a visit to Medicine Hat and takes a motor trip on the north side of the Saskatchewan river with that brilliant and capable irrigationist, one of the ablest in Canada-I do not think there is a better one anywhere-Mr. David Hayes, of the Canada Land and Irrigation Company, he will take him, as he took me, over the route of the canal which ends very close to

Medicine Hat, having started east of the Bow river. It is not connected with the water canal west of the Bow river, as I said, because of lack of money.
In my judgment the first project that should be completed is the Spring Coulee reservoir on the St. Mary river. After the works south of the river are completed, the second project is to proceed to the north and connect up with the main canal of the Canada Land and Irrigation Company so that the water will then syphon east over the Bow River and connect up to the present dry canal east of the Bow river. By that means you would place under irrigation another 100,000 acres of land. In other words north of the ' South Saskatchewan river you would have
245.000	acres of irrigable land, and south of the main line of the South Saskatchewan river you would have 345,000 acres of land also irrigated; in other words, about 600,000 acres of new land.
That will be an additional 600,000 acres of what I call "sure crop" land. It is just as sure crop land as it is possible for land to be. The sun shines nearly all day long. I have never travelled anywhere where I have seen as much sunlight as I saw in southern Alberta. It is no wonder that their flag contains the sun bursting in the sky. The sun as I say, shines nearly all day long. With the sun, the land and the water what place in America could ensure more certain crops than southern Alberta can? For that reason I would not hesitate at all in proceeding with the construction of irrigation works for southern Alberta, both north and south of the main line of the South Saskatchewan . river. [DOT]	.
Now Mr. Speaker, when we know what the land produces-my hon. friend, I believe, told us what the land produces and perhaps I should not repeat it-

The hon. member referred to corn. Vast crops of highgrade corn are grown there. They are developing a market for Alberta corn. It is called Taber sunshine table corn and it is in great demand all through the west and right down to Ontario. In sugar beets they produce up to eighteen tons per acre. In potatoes and all kinds of grains the crops are tremendous on the irrigated land, while across the road, so to speak, on the non-irrigated lands, sage and wild rose and grass grows.
Some will say that you can irrigate that
600.000	acres of land, but what about other millions of acres of land? I believe the time

St. Mary River-Reservoir
is coming, perhaps not yet, when we can do the same thing for Canada that they are doing south of the border. The minister is perhaps better posted on the marvellous results in the half dozen or more states south of the international boundary down to southern Arizona than most hon. members, but I am familiar with it too. There they have built some thirty-six major projects, and they are irrigating over three million acres of new land. On to those three million acres they are transferring over a million citizens, if one counts their families, from the dried-out areas in the dust-bowl. They are going a lot farther; they are now introducing into congress at Washington a bill asking for the expenditure of $1,900,000,000 for irrigation in the California valley drained by the St. Joachim and the Sacramento rivers. That gives the house an idea of what our United States cousins think of the value of irrigation. They have created an enormous market in the last few years for the products and the manufactures of the eastern states. They have created in brand-new business of manufactured goods a new yearly market to the total of over $200 million. That is a lot of new business. That is a lot of jobs in the towns and cities of the eastern states.
If we irrigated 600,000 acres of land that are ready for irrigation in southern Alberta, that are crying out for irrigation, we would create in Alberta alone a market that would affect not only every factory in Ontario, but in Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, because they all manufacture and ship material out there. I have seen and have made it my business to go into the merchant stores, wholesale and retail especially, to ascertain what they had on their shelves that was made in eastern Canada. If they did not 'have a market for it they would not have it there, would they? We can greatly increase that market by irrigating the 600,000 acres of land. But I would not stop there. I think the grand old province of Saskatchewan needs consideration. If there is any province in Canada to-day that needs consideration it is Saskatchewan. Again this year what have they? One-third of their whole southern area depressed by drought. It is heart-breaking. I myself have travelled slowly south from Regina to Estevan, and I have been very muoh depressed with what I saw, all dried-out land upon which farmers, with all the hope that their hearts could have, have sown their seed in the expectation that they would receive some return, but they have received little. It is land that has less than ten inches of water a year; it is land that should have
a minimum of eighteen inches of water a year. That would not be enough to give them great crops, but it would give them somethnig. Take a route straight from the South Saskatchewan river from Riverhurst, right through to IJstevan. There are two million acres of land that could be sure crop land. If it were irrigated it would be sure crop land. Why is it not irrigated? It could be done.
The minister is an engineer; it is fortunate that he is, because he will know better than any other member of the government of the possibilities of engineering. I count on him standing up against anybody telling him that a dam could not be built there. I could build a dam on that river if I were given enough money to do it. That is all that is required. What does it matter if the dam at Riverhurst does cost $5,000,000? What does it matter if the dam has to be 2,000 feet wride, rather thick at the base; what does it matter if it has to be 3,000 feet thick? It does not matter what the width has to be, for they have them on the Tennessee river far wider than that; they have them in the western states far wider than that. What does it matter anyway? The cost is a capital investment. I would build a dam on the South Saskatchewan river somewhere near Riverhurst, and I would build it high enough to divert water not by flow but by pumping. They are doing it down through the United States. Look at the Black Canyon dam in Idaho. That dam is 183 feet high and is irrigating 20,000 acres of land complete and another 20,000 acres of land by pumping. If they can do it there we can do it here, and I would not let anything stop me. I would give those good people between Riverhurst and Estevan a chance to live. I would carry the irrigation works in southern Saskatchewan across that country and provide a sufficient domestic water supply for Regina and Moose Jaw, giving those people also a chance to live, and an opportunity to expand, which they cannot do at the same rate as they would if they had an adequate water supply.
I am sure that if the Minister of Reconstruction would take the bit in his teeth he could do it. He could build irrigation works that would be successful in both southern Alberta and southern Saskatchewan. I am very happy indeed that the minister is here, and it is encouraging, at this late hour, to see the large number of members in the chamber. It goes to show that the heart of the House of Commons is sound. It shows that there are enough men in this House of Commons-I include the lady member alsoms
St. Mary River-Reservoir

who are thoroughly alive to and interested in giving the western provinces a chance for existence. I may say that I was associated vith manufacturing in a big way in eastern Danada, and I know perfectly well what vestem Canada has meant to the building jp not only of that plant with which I had been associated but of every other large manufacturing concern in the east. I know, from close contact with business which came from the west, that the plant with which I was issociated grew from a small beginning to *iuge proportions, and I know that the same 'a true of scores of others, through the develop-nent of the west.
The people of the west have been up against ,t pretty hard. They must have hearts of steel to stand what they have stood. I could not do it. I could not plant crops year in and year out without having any return. Those people must come of a strong and nigged race, and I can well imagine what they would be as a greater buying population if they were assured of huge crops every year: wheat, fifty bushels to the acre; sugar beets, eighteen tons to the acre; corn, 750 cases to the acre, each case containing twenty-four cans; peas, twice as much; dill pickles, sweet potatoes and everything that goes to make for wealth in the country. Millions of new dollars additional could be produced in the west by means of irrigation, wealth which otherwise could not be produced. To me it looks as plain as a-b-c, a matter of ordinary business. The money invested in these projects would give these people a chance to live.
The first job, in my opinion, is the Spring Coulee-St. Mary river reservoir. If we do not tackle that first job to begin with, then I do not see why we should expect our United States cousins to put up with the present situation much longer. They have completed their reservoirs. I know, because I have seen them. They have stored everything they can store and they want more water. Is it not natural, therefore, for them to look across the line and say^ to us, "You are a prodigal people, allowing all this water to run to the sea since 1921; now the time has come to call a halt and we shall have that water ourselves unless you conserve it." And they could take it by the international treaty already signed by us.
In conclusion, let me express my faith in the minister. He is an engineer and he has go; I repeat, if he will take the bit in his teeth and begin by building the Spring Coulee and Chin Coulee project, and the other little reservoirs, and go on to the north side of the river and complete the programme

there, there will be water to the Medicine Hat area and the whole programme will cost about $20 million, which is not much more than we paid for one cruiser. And three or four cruisers belonging to Canada or Great Britain were sunk off the coast of France and we never batted an eyelash. Why should we bat an eyelash at spending $20 million to rehabilitate southern Alberta? Or why should we bat an eyelash at the expenditure of the necessary millions to start a similar programme in Saskatchewan so that we might give the people in Alberta and that part of Saskatchewan a chance to live in the sun?

I have only a minute or two to say what I have to say. I had hoped to make some remarks on this subject, but I may say that the government has rather anticipated this resolution by taking active steps to build the St. Mary river dam, -which, as the resolution suggests, is the first step and the key to the entire project. Plans have been prepared in years gone by, perhaps never very seriously, because it was quite impossible to divert the man-power required by the project during war years. But the plans are well advanced. They are being studied now, and discussions are taking place with the province, because on a project of this kind the province and the federal government must work in complete agreement. It is no small engineering project. As I recall, the dam is 120 feet high, which for an earth dam is a substantial engineering undertaking.
Hon. members will agree with me that the best engineering opinions must be had from men experienced in that type of work. Not only is it a difficult engineering project to build such a dam, but the conditions under which the' dam must operate are very trying in connection with an earth dam. There is a fluctuation of head that is considerable, a fluctuation of head under extreme weather conditions. The danger, as regards a dam of that type, is that the earth will slough as the water level rises and falls, and if that begins nothing can save an earth dam. Therefore the particular material must be studied carefully. It has been studied, and in my opinion the best expert engineering judgment must be brought to bear on the problem. That is being done, and I sincerely hope that a real start can be made toward the construction of the dam during the next building season.
I have given some study to the project. The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNieol) seems to study every interesting project and has given the house a good deal of the back-

Railways and Shipping Committee
ground of this question, and I should like to show the house how much I know about it. But since it is now eleven o'clock I shall have to reserve that for another occasion.

I should just like to say, that one of the two best governments in Canada has been returned to power to-day in one of the best provinces of Canada. The latest report I have indicates that the government in question has elected twenty-one members and is leading in fifteen constituencies, while the opposition is leading in four. It has been a great day for democracy.
Hear, hear.

I hope hon. members will applaud after the next statement. The government of Canada defeated as well, by the representatives of the common people.
It being three minutes after eleven o'clock, the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, October 16, 1945.
